title: Graphs of Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions
overview: Every primary trigonometric function has a reciprocal partner: $\csc x$, $\sec x$ and $\cot x$. You will sketch their graphs from the graphs of sine, cosine and tangent, describe their properties, solve simple equations involving them, and learn not to confuse reciprocal notation ($\csc x$) with inverse notation ($\sin^{-1}x$).
objectives: Sketch $y=\csc x$, $y=\sec x$ and $y=\cot x$ from the graphs of their reciprocals.
State the domain, range, period and asymptotes of each reciprocal function.
Determine values of $x$ for which a reciprocal function takes a given value.
Explain the difference between reciprocal and inverse trigonometric notation.
Model real situations (shadows, wires, light paths) with reciprocal trigonometric functions.

lessons.title: Thinking in reciprocals
lessons.body:
The three **reciprocal trigonometric functions** are

$$\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}\qquad \sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}\qquad \cot x=\frac{1}{\tan x}=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$$

You can sketch each one from its "parent" using four reciprocal rules you already met with rational functions:

| When the parent is… | the reciprocal is… |
|---|---|
| $1$ or $-1$ | the same value ($\frac11=1$, $\frac{1}{-1}=-1$) – the graphs **touch** |
| a small positive number (close to 0) | a **large** positive number |
| a small negative number | a large negative number |
| $0$ | **undefined** – a vertical asymptote |
| increasing | decreasing (and vice versa) |
| positive / negative | the same sign |

So the reciprocal graph lives where the parent lives (same sign), shoots off to infinity at the parent's zeros, and turns around wherever the parent has a max or min of $\pm1$.

lessons.title: The graph of y = csc x
lessons.body:
Start with $y=\sin x$ (dashed below).

* $\sin x=0$ at $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ → **asymptotes** of $y=\csc x$.
* $\sin x=1$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ → $\csc x=1$, a **local minimum** of the "U"-shaped branch.
* $\sin x=-1$ at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ → $\csc x=-1$, a **local maximum** of the downward branch.
* As $x$ moves from $\frac{\pi}{2}$ toward $0$, $\sin x$ shrinks toward $0^+$ so $\csc x$ grows toward $+\infty$.


```plot
title: y = csc x with y = sin x
f: 1/sin(x) | label=y = csc x
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
domain: -pi/4, 9*pi/4
range: -5, 5
xticks: pi
asymptote x: 0, pi, 2*pi
points: (pi/2,1), (3*pi/2,-1)
```


| Property | $y=\csc x$ |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\{x\in\mathbb R\mid x\ne n\pi,\ n\in\mathbb Z\}$ |
| Range | $\{y\mid y\le-1\ \text{or}\ y\ge1\}$ |
| Period | $2\pi$ |
| Asymptotes on $[0,2\pi]$ | $x=0,\ x=\pi,\ x=2\pi$ |

lessons.title: The graph of y = sec x
lessons.body:
Apply the same reasoning to $y=\cos x$: asymptotes where $\cos x=0$, turning points where $\cos x=\pm1$.


```plot
title: y = sec x with y = cos x
f: 1/cos(x) | label=y = sec x
f: cos(x) | dashed; label=y = cos x
domain: -pi/4, 9*pi/4
range: -5, 5
xticks: pi
asymptote x: pi/2, 3*pi/2
points: (0,1), (pi,-1), (2*pi,1)
```


| Property | $y=\sec x$ |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\{x\in\mathbb R\mid x\ne\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\}$ |
| Range | $\{y\mid y\le-1\ \text{or}\ y\ge1\}$ |
| Period | $2\pi$ |
| Asymptotes on $[0,2\pi]$ | $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\ x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ |

Because $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, the secant graph is the cosecant graph shifted $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to the left: $\sec x=\csc\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

lessons.title: The graph of y = cot x
lessons.body:
$\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$.

* **Asymptotes** where $\sin x=0$: $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ (where $\tan x=0$).
* **Zeros** where $\cos x=0$: $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}$ (where $\tan x$ has its asymptotes).
* Where $\tan x$ increases, $\cot x$ decreases. Both equal $\pm1$ at odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{4}$.


```plot
title: y = cot x with y = tan x
f: 1/tan(x) | label=y = cot x
f: tan(x) | dashed; label=y = tan x
domain: -pi/4, 9*pi/4
range: -5, 5
xticks: pi
asymptote x: 0, pi, 2*pi
```


| Property | $y=\cot x$ |
|---|---|
| Domain | $\{x\in\mathbb R\mid x\ne n\pi\}$ |
| Range | $\{y\in\mathbb R\}$ |
| Period | $\pi$ |
| Asymptotes on $[0,2\pi]$ | $x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ |

lessons.title: Values on reciprocal graphs, and reciprocal vs inverse notation
lessons.body:
**Finding $x$ when a reciprocal value is known.** Turn it into a primary ratio:

$$\csc x=3\iff\sin x=\tfrac13\qquad \sec x=2\iff\cos x=\tfrac12\qquad \cot x=-4\iff\tan x=-\tfrac14$$

Then use the inverse key and the CAST rule (or graphing technology) to find all solutions in $[0,2\pi]$. For $\sin x=\frac13$: $x\approx0.34$ and $x\approx\pi-0.34\approx2.80$.

**Reciprocal is not inverse.** The notation is easy to confuse:

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $\csc\frac12$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sin(0.5\text{ rad})}$ – a **number** | $\approx\dfrac{1}{0.4794}\approx2.0858$ |
| $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$ | the **angle** whose sine is $\frac12$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ (also $\frac{5\pi}{6}$, …) |

$\sin^{-1}x$ asks *"which angle?"*; $\csc x$ asks *"what is one over the sine?"* On a calculator, $\csc x$ uses the sine key and then the reciprocal key ($x^{-1}$), while $\sin^{-1}$ is the 2nd function of the sine key.

lessons.title: Modelling with reciprocal functions
lessons.body:
Reciprocal ratios appear naturally whenever a length is the **hypotenuse** or the **adjacent side** divided by a fixed side.

* **Sunlight through the atmosphere.** If the atmosphere has thickness 1 unit and the Sun's rays meet the ground at angle $x$, the rays travel through $y$ units where $\sin x=\frac1y$, so $y=\csc x$. As $x\to0$ (Sun near the horizon) the path grows without bound – that is why sunsets are dimmer and redder.
* **Shadows.** A tree of height $h$ casts a shadow $s$ with $\tan x=\frac{h}{s}$, so $s=h\cot x$. As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}$ (Sun overhead) the shadow shrinks to 0; as $x\to0$ the shadow becomes infinitely long.
* **Swimming across a pool.** Diving in and swimming diagonally across a pool of width $w$ at angle $x$ to the width gives distance $d=w\sec x$.
* **Swing rides.** The angle of a swing satisfies $\cot x=\dfrac{rg}{v^2}$.

keyTerms.definition: $\cot x=\frac{1}{\tan x}=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$; undefined where $\sin x=0$.
One of $\csc$, $\sec$, $\cot$ – the reciprocal of a primary trigonometric function.
$\sin^{-1}x$, $\cos^{-1}x$, $\tan^{-1}x$ give an **angle** with the given ratio – not a reciprocal.

formulas.name: Reciprocal identities
formulas.latex: \csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x},\quad \sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x},\quad \cot x=\frac{1}{\tan x}
formulas.meaning: Convert a reciprocal equation into a primary-ratio equation.

formulas.name: Cotangent as a quotient
formulas.meaning: Zeros where $\cos x=0$, asymptotes where $\sin x=0$.

workedExamples.title: Solving csc x = 3
workedExamples.problem: Determine all $x\in[0,2\pi]$ with $\csc x=3$, to two decimal places. What happens where $\csc x=-1$?
steps: Sine is also positive in quadrant II: $x=\pi-0.3398\approx2.80$.
$\csc x=-1$ when $\sin x=-1$, i.e. at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ – the only place in $[0,2\pi]$; here the cosecant and sine graphs touch.

workedExamples.title: Reciprocal versus inverse
workedExamples.problem: Explain the difference between $\csc\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)$ and evaluate each.
steps: $\csc\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sin(0.7071\text{ rad})}$ – one over the sine of the **angle** $0.7071$ rad.
workedExamples.answer: $\csc\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx1.539$ (a single number); $\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ (an angle, one of many).

workedExamples.title: Shadow length
workedExamples.problem: A tree 12 m tall casts a shadow of length $s$ when the Sun's angle of elevation is $x$. Show that $s=12\cot x$ and describe the graph on $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
steps: In the right triangle, the tree is opposite $x$ and the shadow is adjacent: $\tan x=\frac{12}{s}$.

Rearrange: $s=\frac{12}{\tan x}=12\cot x$.

```plot
f: 12/tan(x) | label=s = 12 cot x
domain: 0.05, pi/2
range: 0, 60
xticks: pi
ticks: 0.25, 10
```
As $x\to0^+$, $\cot x\to\infty$: the shadow becomes extremely long (Sun at the horizon).
As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^-$, $\cot x\to0$: the shadow disappears (Sun overhead).
workedExamples.answer: $s=12\cot x$, decreasing from very large values to 0 across $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

misconceptions.fact: $\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}$ is a reciprocal (a number). $\sin^{-1}x$ is an inverse – it returns an **angle**.

misconceptions.myth: $\sec x$ is the reciprocal of $\sin x$ because both start with 's'.
misconceptions.fact: Each pair contains exactly one 'co': $\csc$ ↔ $\sin$, $\sec$ ↔ $\cos$, $\cot$ ↔ $\tan$. So $\sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}$, not $\frac{1}{\sin x}$.

misconceptions.myth: The reciprocal graph has asymptotes where the parent graph has asymptotes.
misconceptions.fact: Asymptotes of the reciprocal occur where the parent is **zero**. Where tangent has asymptotes, cotangent has **zeros**.
Cosecant and secant are unbounded, so they have no amplitude; their range is $y\le-1$ or $y\ge1$.
2nd-COS is $\cos^{-1}$. Evaluate $\cos 2$ first, then take the reciprocal.

realWorld.title: Radar antennas
realWorld.body: Engineers shape the radiation pattern of radar antenna arrays using a cosecant function so that energy is spread to where aircraft actually are, not wasted on empty airspace.

realWorld.title: Awnings
realWorld.body: An awning that must completely shade a 2 m window when the Sun is at elevation $x$ needs to project $d=2\cot x$ from the wall.

realWorld.title: Lighthouse beams
realWorld.body: A lighthouse 500 m from a straight cliff rotates its beam through angle $x$; the distance to the spot lit on the cliff is $500\sec x$.

realWorld.title: Swing rides
realWorld.body: On a swing ride, $\cot x=\frac{rg}{v^2}$ relates the swing angle to the speed $v$ and the distance $r$ from the centre.

practice.question: Determine all $x\in[0,2\pi]$ with $\csc x=5$, to two decimal places.
practice.hint: $\sin x=\frac15$; sine positive in quadrants I and II.

practice.question: Determine all $x\in[0,2\pi]$ with $\cot x=-4$.
practice.hint: $\tan x=-0.25$; tangent negative in quadrants II and IV.

practice.question: Explain the difference between $\cot1$ and $\tan^{-1}(1)$ and evaluate each.
practice.hint: One is a reciprocal of a ratio; the other is an angle.

practice.question: Describe the graph of $y=\sec x$ as a transformation of $y=\csc x$. Is there more than one transformation?
practice.solution: A translation $\frac{\pi}{2}$ left: $\sec x=\csc(x+\frac{\pi}{2})$. Since the period is $2\pi$, a translation $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ right also works (and any of these plus multiples of $2\pi$).

practice.question: For what values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ does $\cos x=\sec x$?
Where do $y=\tan x$ and $y=\cot x$ intersect on $[0,2\pi]$?

summary: $\csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}$, $\sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}$, $\cot x=\frac{1}{\tan x}$.
Reciprocal graphs have vertical asymptotes at the zeros of the parent and touch the parent where it equals $\pm1$.
$\csc$ and $\sec$ have period $2\pi$ and range $y\le-1$ or $y\ge1$; $\cot$ has period $\pi$ and range $\mathbb R$.
Solve reciprocal equations by converting to the primary ratio.

questions.text: Determine all values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ such that $\csc x={{c}}$. Round to two decimal places and explain your method.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\csc x={{c}}\iff\sin x=\dfrac{1}{ {{c}} }\approx{{1/c:4}}$.

Quadrant I: $x=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{ {{c}} }\right)\approx{{asin(1/c):3}}$.

Sine is also positive in quadrant II: $x=\pi-{{asin(1/c):3}}\approx{{pi-asin(1/c):3}}$.

rubric.point: Correct second solution using quadrant II

questions.text: Determine all values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ such that $\sec x={{c}}$, to two decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\cos x=\dfrac{1}{ {{c}} }$. Quadrant I: $x=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{ {{c}} }\right)\approx{{acos(1/c):3}}$.

Cosine is also positive in quadrant IV: $x=2\pi-{{acos(1/c):3}}\approx{{2*pi-acos(1/c):3}}$.

questions.text: Determine all values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ such that $\cot x=-{{c}}$, to two decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\tan x=-\dfrac{1}{ {{c}} }$. The reference angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{ {{c}} }\right)\approx{{atan(1/c):3}}$.

Tangent is negative in quadrants II and IV:

$x=\pi-{{atan(1/c):3}}\approx{{pi-atan(1/c):3}}$ and $x=2\pi-{{atan(1/c):3}}\approx{{2*pi-atan(1/c):3}}$.

rubric.point: Both solutions in the correct quadrants

questions.text: (a) Explain the difference between $\csc\dfrac{1}{ {{n}} }$ and $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{ {{n}} }\right)$. (b) Determine a value for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\csc\frac{1}{ {{n}} }$ is the reciprocal of the sine of the angle $\frac{1}{ {{n}} }$ rad – a single number. $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{ {{n}} }\right)$ is an angle whose sine equals $\frac{1}{ {{n}} }$; there are infinitely many such angles.

(b) $\csc\frac{1}{ {{n}} }=\dfrac{1}{\sin({{1/n:4}})}\approx{{1/sin(1/n):4}}$.

$\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{ {{n}} }\right)\approx{{asin(1/n):4}}$ rad (another answer is $\pi-{{asin(1/n):4}}$).

rubric.point: Explains inverse meaning (an angle, many answers)

questions.text: Explain how to sketch the graph of $y=\csc x$ on $[0,2\pi]$ using the graph of $y=\sin x$. Your explanation should identify where the graphs intersect, where the asymptotes are and why, and how the shape of each branch is determined. State the domain, range and period of $y=\csc x$.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Sketch $y=\sin x$.
2. The graphs intersect where $\sin x=\pm1$ (since $\frac{1}{1}=1$ and $\frac{1}{-1}=-1$): $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},1\right)$ and $\left(\frac{3\pi}{2},-1\right)$.
3. Where $\sin x=0$ ($x=0,\pi,2\pi$), $\csc x$ is undefined; as $\sin x\to0$, $\csc x$ grows without bound, so these are vertical asymptotes.
4. From $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ toward $0$ or toward $\pi$, $\sin x$ decreases toward $0^+$, so $\csc x$ increases toward $+\infty$ – a U-shaped branch above with minimum $(\frac{\pi}{2},1)$. Between $\pi$ and $2\pi$ the branch opens downward with maximum $(\frac{3\pi}{2},-1)$.

Domain $x\ne n\pi$; range $y\le-1$ or $y\ge1$; period $2\pi$.

rubric.point: Asymptotes at zeros of sine with reason

questions.text: Copy and complete a summary of $y=\sec x$ and $y=\cot x$: for each, give the domain, range, period, the equations of the asymptotes on $[0,2\pi]$, and any zeros on $[0,2\pi]$.
questions.modelAnswer:
$y=\sec x$: domain $x\ne\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi$; range $y\le-1$ or $y\ge1$; period $2\pi$; asymptotes $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$; no zeros.

$y=\cot x$: domain $x\ne n\pi$; range $\mathbb R$; period $\pi$; asymptotes $x=0$, $x=\pi$, $x=2\pi$; zeros at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: (a) Describe the graph of $y=\sec x$ as a transformation of $y=\csc x$. (b) Is there more than one transformation that works? Explain.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Because $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, taking reciprocals gives $\sec x=\csc\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$: the secant graph is the cosecant graph translated $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to the left.

(b) Yes. Both graphs have period $2\pi$, so a translation of $\frac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi$ left (e.g. $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ to the right) also works. A reflection in the $y$-axis combined with a translation also works, since $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$ and so $\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\sec x$.

rubric.point: Correct translation with justification from identity
States other translations due to period

questions.text: When the Sun is at an angle of elevation $x$, a tree of height {{h}} m casts a shadow of length $s$ metres.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the graph of $s$ on $x\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and interpret it as $x$ approaches 0 and $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The tree is opposite $x$ and the shadow adjacent: $\tan x=\dfrac{ {{h}} }{s}$, so $s=\dfrac{ {{h}} }{\tan x}={{h}}\cot x$.

(b) At $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$: $s={{h}}\cot\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\approx{{h/tan(pi/n):3}}$ m.

(c) As $x\to0^+$, $\cot x\to+\infty$: the shadow becomes very long (Sun near the horizon). As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^-$, $\cot x\to0$: the shadow shrinks to nothing (Sun directly overhead). The graph decreases throughout $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ with a vertical asymptote at $x=0$.

rubric.point: Shows s = h cot x from the triangle
Interprets both ends with the asymptote

questions.text: An awning shades a window of height {{h}} m. It projects a distance $d$ from the wall so that the window is completely shaded when the Sun's elevation is $x$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How far must the awning project if $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The window height is opposite $x$ and $d$ is adjacent: $\tan x=\frac{ {{h}} }{d}$, so $d={{h}}\cot x$.

(b) $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$: $d={{h}}\cot\frac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{ {{h}} }{\sqrt3}\approx{{h/sqrt(3):3}}$ m.

(c) As $x\to0$, $d\to\infty$ (no awning could shade the window when the Sun is very low). As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}$, $d\to0$ (the Sun is overhead, so almost no projection is needed).

questions.text: A sailboat's mast is {{h}} m high. A wire of length $l$ metres runs from the bow to the top of the mast, making an angle of inclination $x$ with the deck.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Interpret the graph of $l$ on $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ as $x\to0$ and $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The mast is opposite $x$, the wire is the hypotenuse: $\sin x=\dfrac{ {{h}} }{l}$, so $l=\dfrac{ {{h}} }{\sin x}={{h}}\csc x$.

(b) At $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$: $l={{h}}\csc\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\approx{{h/sin(pi/n):3}}$ m.

(c) As $x\to0$, $\csc x\to\infty$: the wire would need to be extremely long (attached very far from the mast). As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\csc x\to1$, so $l\to{{h}}$ m: the wire becomes vertical, the same length as the mast.

questions.text: A lifeguard at one end of a pool of width $w$ runs along the length to a point $P$, then dives in and swims a distance $d$ to a swimmer at the opposite corner $S$. The swimming path makes angle $x$ with the width of the pool. The pool length is $l=2w$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the range of values that $x$ may take.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the range of values of $d$ in terms of $w$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a reason the lifeguard might swim rather than run all the way.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The width $w$ is adjacent to $x$ and $d$ is the hypotenuse: $\cos x=\frac{w}{d}$, so $d=w\sec x$.

(b) If $P$ is directly across from $S$, $x=0$. If $P$ is at the far end (where the lifeguard started), the horizontal leg is $l=2w$, so $\tan x=\frac{2w}{w}=2$ and $x=\tan^{-1}2\approx1.11$. So $0\le x\le1.11$.

(c) $d=w\sec x$ increases on this interval: from $w\sec0=w$ to $w\sec(1.107)=w\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5\,w\approx2.24w$.

(d) Running all the way round means covering the length and then the width on foot ($3w$ in total) with no way to reach the swimmer from the deck; diving in earlier lets the lifeguard reach the swimmer sooner along a shorter overall path, even though swimming is slower than running.

rubric.point: Correct interval for x including tan⁻¹2

questions.text: On a swing ride, the angle $x$ that a swing makes with the vertical satisfies $\cot x=\dfrac{rg}{v^2}$, where $r$ is the distance (m) from the centre of rotation, $g=9.8$ m/s² and $v$ is the speed (m/s). A swing is {{r}} m from the centre and moves at {{v}} m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine $x$ to the nearest hundredth of a radian.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If $r$ is doubled at the same speed, does the angle double? Justify.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the speed is doubled at the same $r$, does the angle halve? Justify.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\cot x=\dfrac{ {{r}}(9.8)}{ {{v}}^2}\approx{{r*9.8/v^2:4}}$, so $\tan x\approx{{v^2/(r*9.8):4}}$ and $x\approx{{atan(v^2/(r*9.8)):3}}$ rad.

(b) Doubling $r$ doubles $\cot x$: $\tan x\approx{{v^2/(2*r*9.8):4}}$, $x\approx{{atan(v^2/(2*r*9.8)):3}}$. The angle does **not** halve or double – the relationship between $x$ and $\cot x$ is not linear.

(c) Doubling $v$ divides $\cot x$ by 4, giving $x\approx{{atan(4*v^2/(r*9.8)):3}}$, which is not twice the original angle.

questions.text: A lighthouse with a rotating beam is {{D}} m south of a straight coastal cliff that runs west to east. The beam rotates through angle $x$ measured from due north.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find a relation for the distance $d$ from the lighthouse to the lit point on the cliff.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The perpendicular distance {{D}} m is adjacent to $x$ and the beam's path is the hypotenuse: $d={{D}}\sec x$.

(b) At $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$: $d={{D}}\sec\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\approx{{D/cos(pi/n):4}}$ m.

(c) As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}$ the beam becomes parallel to the cliff and never reaches it: $d\to\infty$, a vertical asymptote at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: Solve each equation on $[0,2\pi]$ and explain your reasoning: (a) $\cos x=\sec x$; (b) $\tan x=\cot x$; (c) $\csc x=\sin x$.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\cos x=\frac{1}{\cos x}\Rightarrow\cos^2x=1\Rightarrow\cos x=\pm1$: $x=0,\pi,2\pi$.

(b) $\tan x=\frac{1}{\tan x}\Rightarrow\tan^2x=1\Rightarrow\tan x=\pm1$: $x=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4},\frac{7\pi}{4}$.

(c) $\sin^2x=1\Rightarrow\sin x=\pm1$: $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}$. These are the points where a function and its reciprocal both equal $\pm1$.

questions.text: Consider $y=\csc 2x$. Predict the values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ at which vertical asymptotes occur, and state the period. Justify your prediction.
questions.modelAnswer:
Asymptotes occur where $\sin2x=0$: $2x=n\pi\Rightarrow x=\frac{n\pi}{2}$. On $[0,2\pi]$: $x=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi$.

Period: $\frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$, half that of $y=\csc x$, because the parent $\sin2x$ has period $\pi$.

questions.text: When the Sun is directly overhead its rays pass through 1 unit of atmosphere. When the Sun is inclined at angle $x$ to Earth's surface the rays pass through $y$ units. (a) Explain why $y=\csc x$. (b) Describe what happens to $y$ as $x\to0$ and explain why this makes sense. (c) State two assumptions in this model.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The atmosphere has vertical thickness 1, opposite angle $x$; the ray's path $y$ is the hypotenuse: $\sin x=\frac1y$, so $y=\frac{1}{\sin x}=\csc x$.

(b) As $x\to0$, $\sin x\to0$, so $y\to\infty$: the Sun's rays travel through more and more air as the Sun approaches the horizon, which is why sunlight is weaker at sunrise and sunset.

(c) Earth's surface is flat; the atmosphere is uniform and ends at a fixed height (so the path is a straight line through a constant-thickness layer).

questions.text: Use graphs of $y=\csc^2x$ and $y=\cot^2x$ (or a table of values) to decide whether $\csc^2x=\cot^2x$ is an identity. If it is not, find a similar equation that is an identity and prove it.
questions.modelAnswer:
It is not an identity: at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\csc^2x=1$ but $\cot^2x=0$. The graphs have the same shape but $y=\csc^2x$ is always 1 unit higher.

Conjecture: $\csc^2x=1+\cot^2x$.

Proof: start with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and divide by $\sin^2x$ ($\sin x\ne0$):
$$1+\frac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}=\frac{1}{\sin^2x}\ \Rightarrow\ 1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x.$$
